lead: Cloud computing pools machines in a few large data centres. Some jobs cannot wait for that distance: a toll-gate camera, a phone running a speech model, a factory sensor. Edge computing moves computation to a small node beside the data; mobile cloud computing moves it off the phone to a nearby or remote server. Both give up some of the cloud's capacity in return for lower delay and less bandwidth used. Both appear in video surveillance, number-plate reading, augmented reality and factory control. The data centre still runs long jobs, training and archives.
prereq: You need: the layered architecture of Chapter 1.5 and the deployment models of Chapter 1.7.

sections.h3: Edge computing: the node beside the data

blocks.text: Edge computing places computation close to where data is produced instead of a distant data centre. The reason is delay. Light in glass travels at about 2 × 108 m/s, so 1,000 km of fibre costs at least 5 ms one way and 10 ms round trip before any device works. Routing, queues and a mobile radio add more. A toll-gate camera talking to a cloud region 1,000 km away commonly sees 60 ms round trip, while the service may allow 50 ms.

An edge node is a small server in the same street, factory or building as the sensors. Typical: a few CPU cores, 8–16 GB memory, sometimes a small accelerator, 30–100 W, no air-conditioned room, no technician on site. Size does not make it edge. It is edge when it sits next to the data source and is managed from the cloud as one fleet: same software image pushed to thousands of nodes, health and error reports flowing back, bad update rolled back from a central console.
That second condition is what exams test. A server in your basement, patched by hand, is a local server, not an edge node.

Between sensors and data centre there is usually a middle layer. Fog computing is the name for nodes at regional level: a telecom aggregation site or ISP point of presence, tens of kilometres away, bigger than an edge node and smaller than a cloud region. Only a few syllabi use the word fog; two lines are enough.

Each tier trades delay for capacity. A camera sees about 5 ms to an edge node in the same street, 25 ms to a regional fog node in the same state, and 60 ms to a cloud data centre. Run the job at the lowest tier whose total time fits the deadline and whose operators may see the data.

blocks.where: T_total is the time from the sensor producing a frame to the answer arriving, in ms; T_net is the round-trip network delay between sensor and tier, in ms; T_comp is the model's compute time on that tier, in ms.

sections.h3: Mobile cloud computing: offloading from the phone

blocks.text: Mobile cloud computing (MCC) is the phone, radio network and cloud working as one system: heavy work leaves the phone and only the result comes back. A phone has a small battery and a processor that must stay cool, so a large model run locally for two minutes drains charge and heats the case. The same work on a server uses a fraction of the phone's energy.

The offloading decision compares three quantities: energy, delay and bandwidth. Local execution costs energy = CPU power × time. Offloading costs the radio energy for bytes sent up and result sent down, plus energy of staying awake while waiting. Offload when radio cost plus waiting is less than local cost and the round trip fits what the user will tolerate.
A cloudlet is a small data centre one wireless hop from the phone — same campus, mall or office — so the round trip is a few milliseconds instead of tens. It makes offloading worthwhile indoors.

Four things make MCC hard. Links drop, and a train entering a tunnel kills an offload in flight. Batteries vary. Phones differ in chip and operating system. Mobile data is sold per gigabyte, so an offload that saves battery can cost money on a metered plan; on Wi-Fi the decision may flip.

items: Edge wins when deadline is a few milliseconds, data is bulky (video), backhaul is expensive or absent, or data must stay on site for privacy.
Cloud wins for long jobs, model training, archives and bursty load, because it can hold thousands of machines and cheap storage and is paid by the hour.
Usual pattern: train the model in the cloud, push it to the edge fleet, send alerts and logs back to the cloud.

blocks.text: The edge is a thin layer with limited power and no technician. The cloud does not disappear. Its role shifts to the later stages — collecting logs, retraining the model, keeping archives — while the first stage of the job runs on the edge.

examples.question: A city runs 1,000 toll-gate cameras, each producing a 2 MB frame twice a second. The number-plate model needs 20 ms of compute. It can run on the camera (90 ms end to end), in a cloud region with 60 ms round trip, or on an edge node 5 ms away. The service level requires an answer within 50 ms. (a) Which placement meets the deadline, and by how much? (b) What backhaul does sending every frame to the cloud need? (c) If only one 50 KB alert per camera every 10 seconds leaves the edge node, what backhaul is needed, and by what factor does it fall?
steps: Edge: T_total = 5 + 20 = 25 ms ≤ 50, passes with 25 ms spare.
Every frame: 1,000 × 2 = 2,000 frames/s. 2,000 × 2 MB = 4,000 MB/s = 4 GB/s. In bits: 4,000 × 8 = 32,000 Mbit/s = 32 Gbit/s.
Only alerts: 1,000 ÷ 10 = 100 alerts/s. 100 × 50 KB = 5,000 KB/s = 5 MB/s = 40 Mbit/s.
examples.answer: Only the edge node meets 50 ms, at 25 ms with 25 ms spare; every frame needs 32 Gbit/s, only alerts need 40 Mbit/s, 800 times less.

mb_per_s = frames_per_s * 2

alert_mb_per_s = alerts_per_s * 50 / 1000
print(alert_mb_per_s * 8)
print(32000 / 40)

traps: Calling any nearby server 'edge'. A node is edge only if it is close to the data source and managed from the cloud as one fleet. Being small proves nothing.
Treating MCC as a website opened on a phone. MCC is offloading of computation; a responsive web page is not offloading.
Unit slips in backhaul: MB/s to Mbit/s is × 8, Mbit to Gbit is ÷ 1,000. So 4 GB/s is 32 Gbit/s, not 4 Gbit/s.
Forgetting compute time, or counting the round trip twice. Use T_total = T_net + T_comp, where T_net is already a round trip.
Claiming edge replaces the cloud. Edge nodes have 30–100 W and no technician; training, archives and long jobs stay in the data centre.

quiz.q: Define edge computing, and state the two conditions that make a node an edge node.
quiz.a: Edge computing is computation placed close to where the data is produced. A node is an edge node when it is near the data source and is managed from the cloud as part of one fleet.

quiz.q: A cloud server is ten times faster than an edge node, yet a 50 ms deadline job cannot run there. Explain why.
quiz.a: Delay is set by distance, not by CPU speed. The cloud round trip is about 60 ms, already over the 50 ms budget before any compute is added. The edge node's 5 ms round trip leaves 45 ms for compute, so a slow chip still fits.

quiz.q: A model takes 30 ms of compute. Cloud round trip is 70 ms, edge round trip is 4 ms, deadline is 60 ms. Which tier fits, and by what margin?
quiz.a: Cloud: T_total = 70 + 30 = 100 ms > 60, fails. Edge: T_total = 4 + 30 = 34 ms ≤ 60, passes with 60 − 34 = 26 ms to spare.

quiz.q: 500 cameras each send one 1.5 MB frame per second to the cloud. What backhaul is needed, in Gbit/s?
quiz.a: 500 × 1.5 MB = 750 MB/s. In bits: 750 × 8 = 6,000 Mbit/s = 6 Gbit/s.

quiz.q: An offload saves 40% of the energy that this task would otherwise use on the phone. Why might the user still refuse it?
quiz.a: The saving is in battery energy, not money or reliability. On a metered mobile plan the upload costs rupees per gigabyte, the link may drop mid-transfer, and the data may be private. On Wi-Fi the same offload may be accepted.

quiz.q: 'We run our model on a rack server in the basement, patched by hand, so we do edge computing.' Critique this statement.
quiz.a: It meets only one condition. The server is near the data, but it is not managed from the cloud as part of one fleet, so it does not scale to many sites, cannot be updated or rolled back centrally, and its health is invisible. It is a local server, not an edge node.

beyond: Not for the exam. 5G networks now host applications inside the telecom operator itself, under the name multi-access edge computing, which merges the fog and edge layers into one operator-run tier. Fleet tools built on containers, such as KubeEdge and OpenYurt, extend a Kubernetes cluster onto edge nodes so thousands of sites are managed like one data centre. Federated learning trains a model across phones without sending raw data up, which answers part of the privacy objection to offloading.
